title: Preguntar per informació / Asking for information
bridge: In Catalan, asking for information at the airport often involves using the verb 'voler' (to want) instead of 'needing' or 'looking for', which is more common in English. Additionally, Catalan speakers frequently use the formal 'vostè' form when addressing strangers, unlike English where 'you' is universally used. Be mindful of the word order in questions, as Catalan places the verb before the subject in yes/no questions, unlike English.
rule: To ask for information in Catalan, use the structure: 'Vostè em pot dir...' (Can you tell me...) or 'Vull saber...' (I want to know...). For yes/no questions, invert the subject and verb, e.g., 'És aquest el vol per Barcelona?' (Is this the flight to Barcelona?). Always use formal 'vostè' when addressing airport staff unless invited to use 'tu'.

title: Fer una reserva / Making a reservation
bridge: In Catalan, making a hotel reservation involves using formal language and specific phrases. Unlike English, where 'book a room' is common, Catalan uses 'fer una reserva' or 'reservar una habitació'. Be careful with false friends like 'habitació' (room), which is pronounced differently and has a distinct accent mark. Also, Catalan often uses the formal 'vostè' (you) in customer service, whereas English typically uses 'you' without formality.
rule: To make a reservation in Catalan, use the phrase 'Vull reservar una habitació' (I want to book a room). Specify the type of room with 'individual' (single), 'doble' (double), or 'suite'. Use 'per a' (for) to indicate the number of nights, e.g., 'per a dues nits' (for two nights). Always use formal language with hotel staff, addressing them as 'senyor/senyora' (sir/madam) or using 'vostè'.

title: Demanar menjar i beguda / Ordering Food and Drinks
bridge: In Catalan, when ordering food and drinks, the verb 'demanar' (to ask for) is commonly used, whereas in English, we often use 'Can I have...' or 'I'll take...'. Be careful with the word order: in Catalan, the object usually comes before the verb in questions, unlike in English. Also, note that Catalan uses the formal 'vostè' form in restaurants, which is similar to 'you' in English but implies respect.
rule: To order food and drinks in Catalan, use the structure: 'Vull...' (I want...) or 'Em pots donar...' (Can you give me...). For questions, use 'Podria tenir...' (Could I have...). Remember to use the formal 'vostè' form when addressing the waiter. Common phrases include 'L'account, si us plau' (The bill, please) and 'Bon profit!' (Enjoy your meal).

Instead, use 'Vull...' or 'Podria tenir...' to sound more natural. The error occurs because of the direct translation habit, which doesn't account for the different verb usage in Catalan.

title: Comprar medicaments / Buying Medicine
bridge: In Catalan, when buying medicine at the pharmacy, you'll notice that the verb 'comprar' (to buy) is used similarly to English, but the vocabulary for common ailments and medications differs. For instance, 'ibuprofeno' is the Catalan word for ibuprofen, and 'antibiótic' for antibiotic. Be careful with false friends like 'constipat', which means constipated in Catalan, not having a cold as 'constipated' might imply in British English.
rule: To ask for medicine, use the phrase 'Vull comprar...' (I want to buy...) followed by the medication name. For describing symptoms, use 'Tinc...' (I have...) + symptom. Remember, in Catalan, adjectives often come after the noun, unlike in English. For example, 'medicament fort' (strong medicine).

title: Comprar al supermercat / Shopping at the supermarket
bridge: In Catalan, unlike English, you often use the verb 'agafar' (to take) instead of 'buy' when referring to selecting items in a supermarket. Additionally, Catalan uses the preposition 'a' to indicate the place where you are shopping, which might feel unnatural for English speakers. Be careful with false friends like 'caixa' (checkout) instead of 'box'.
rule: To talk about shopping at the supermarket in Catalan, use the structure 'Agafar + item' to express selecting items. For asking prices, use 'Quan costa...?' (How much does... cost?). When specifying quantities, place the number before the noun. Remember to use 'a' to indicate the location of shopping, as in 'anar al supermercat' (to go to the supermarket).

title: Comprar bitllets / Buying Tickets
bridge: In Catalan, buying tickets for public transport often involves specific vocabulary and phrases that differ from English. For instance, 'bitllet' (ticket) is masculine, unlike the English 'ticket,' which doesn't have gender. Additionally, Catalan uses the verb 'comprar' (to buy) followed by a direct object, whereas in English, you might say 'get a ticket' or 'purchase a ticket.' Be mindful of the gender agreement in Catalan, as it affects articles and adjectives.
rule: To buy tickets in Catalan, use the phrase 'Vull comprar un bitllet' (I want to buy a ticket). The verb 'comprar' is conjugated based on the subject. For example, 'Jo compro' (I buy), 'Tu compres' (You buy). The noun 'bitllet' is masculine, so use 'un' (a/an) before it. For multiple tickets, say 'bitllets' (plural) and use 'uns' or a number. Common phrases include 'Bitllet d’anada i tornada' (Round-trip ticket) and 'Bitllet senzill' (One-way ticket).

title: Presentacions / Introductions
bridge: In Catalan, introductions often include the verb 'ser' (to be) for professions and 'estar' (to be) for temporary states, unlike English where 'to be' is used for both. Be careful with the formal 'vostè' vs. informal 'tu', as English uses 'you' for both. Also, Catalan greetings like 'Hola' are more versatile than English 'Hi' or 'Hello'.
rule: To introduce yourself in Catalan, use 'Em dic [name]' (My name is [name]). For professions, use 'Sóc [profession]'. For temporary states, use 'Estic [state]'. Always use 'Hola' for greetings and 'Adéu' for goodbyes. Remember to use 'vostè' for formal situations and 'tu' for informal ones.

title: Demanar begudes / Ordering Drinks
bridge: In Catalan, when ordering drinks in a café, the structure is similar to English, but the verb 'voler' (to want) is often replaced with 'vull' (I want) in a more direct and informal way. Unlike English, Catalan uses the definite article 'el' or 'la' before the drink name, which might feel unnatural at first. Be careful not to directly translate 'I would like' as it can sound overly formal in Catalan.
rule: To order drinks in Catalan, use the structure: 'Vull + article + drink name'. For example, 'Vull un cafè' (I want a coffee). The article 'un' (a/an) is optional but commonly used. For specific quantities, use numbers: 'Vull dos tès' (I want two teas). Remember, Catalan speakers often omit 'si us plau' (please) in casual settings, but it’s polite to include it when learning.

title: Trucar i enviar missatges / Calling and Texting
bridge: In Catalan, unlike English, the verb 'trucar' is used for both 'to call' and 'to knock'. Be careful not to confuse it with 'dir' (to say). Additionally, Catalan uses the verb 'enviar' for 'to send' a message, similar to English, but the preposition 'a' is required before the recipient, which is a key difference.
rule: To talk about calling and texting in Catalan, use 'trucar a' for 'to call someone' and 'enviar un missatge a' for 'to send a message to someone'. The preposition 'a' is always used before the recipient. For example, 'Truco a Maria' means 'I call Maria'. For texting, 'Envio un missatge a Joan' means 'I send a message to Joan'.

title: Frases d'emergència / Emergency Phrases
bridge: In Catalan, emergency phrases often use formal commands or polite requests, unlike English where direct commands are more common. For example, 'Truca a la policia' (Call the police) uses the verb 'trucar' (to call), which is more formal than the English 'call.' Be careful with false friends like 'emergència' (emergency), which is pronounced differently and has a distinct stress pattern compared to English.
rule: Emergency phrases in Catalan typically use the imperative form of verbs for direct commands or the phrase 'Pot/Podria...?' for polite requests. Common verbs include 'trucar' (to call), 'ajudar' (to help), and 'anar' (to go). Remember to use formal forms when addressing strangers or in serious situations. Key phrases often include location indicators like 'aquí' (here) or 'allà' (there).
